title: Sebastian and the Wardrobe
premise: Isandro Almeida has spent seven years writing postcards to her mother at an address that burned down, a ritual that lets her grieve without ever saying anything true aloud. At the funeral of a family friend, a stranger calls her household by its old name—the Almeidas of the Wardrobe, keepers of documents hidden from the dictatorship—and Isandro learns her quiet childhood was built on her mother's silence about a betrayal that sent a man to prison in their place. Following the stranger's clues back to the coastal town she fled, she uncovers letters, a hidden wardrobe of papers, and the truth that her mother loved the man they destroyed. Choosing justice over the family's fragile peace, Isandro publishes the archive and finally writes one last postcard—to herself—at the address where the story began.
about_author: S. M. Underhill is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the personal papers of families displaced by political upheaval. They write literary fiction about inheritance, secrecy, and the small domestic objects that carry history.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Isandro, a translator in the city who mails weekly postcards to her mother's burned-down address, signed with words she never said in life. Her days are careful, rented, anonymous. When news arrives that Tia Rosa has died, Isandro must decide whether to attend the funeral—her first return to family in years. Beat: loneliness disguised as order.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the funeral, POV Isandro. A gaunt stranger named Duarte greets mourners by calling the family 'the Almeidas of the Wardrobe'—a name Isandro has never heard. Her uncle Silvestre goes white and hustles the man out. Isandro catches only Duarte's parting whisper: 'Ask your mother what she kept.' But her mother is dead; the question has nowhere to land. Beat: the crack in the wall.

chapters.title: A Tenant's Inventory
chapters.summary: POV Isandro, back in her flat, trying to resume routine. She inventories her mother's surviving boxes—linens, recipes, a locked writing case no key fits. Uncle Silvestre phones, urging her not to 'dig up what the fire already buried,' which only confirms there is something to bury. She finds Duarte's number scrawled on the funeral card. Beat: curiosity hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Duarte
chapters.summary: POV alternates between Isandro and Duarte's letters. Meeting in a train-station café, Duarte reveals he was the son of Tomás Ribeiro, the man convicted of smuggling dissidents' papers in 1974—a crime the Almeida family knew was theirs. He believes his father's exculpatory letters survive somewhere in the old house. He doesn't accuse; he asks. Beat: sympathy complicated by suspicion.

chapters.title: The House on Rua das Acácias
chapters.summary: POV Isandro returns to the coastal town, staying in the half-abandoned family house above the scorched lot where her mother's home stood. The town remembers her as 'the daughter who left.' Uncle Silvestre arrives unannounced, offering money to go back to the city. Their confrontation exposes his fear—not of scandal, but of what their mother did to protect them. Beat: duty pulling against truth.

chapters.title: What the Fire Spared
chapters.summary: POV Isandro, searching the ruins and the house. In the cellar she finds the wardrobe—an enormous carved armoire—with a false back concealing bundles of letters: her mother's correspondence with Tomás Ribeiro, tender, guilty, decades long. The last letter, dated after his conviction, is unfinished. Isandro realizes her mother's postcard ritual was inherited from Tomás's habit of writing to an address that couldn't answer. Beat: grief reorganized around love.

chapters.title: Silvestre's Version
chapters.summary: POV shifts partly to Silvestre via a long confession scene. He admits he informed on Tomás in 1974—not for ideology, but jealousy and panic—and let his sister carry the secret while he built a respectable life. He begs Isandro to burn the letters: exposure now would ruin grandchildren who are innocent. His plea is genuinely loving and genuinely self-serving. Beat: the antagonist made human.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Key
chapters.summary: POV Isandro, paralyzed between justice and mercy. She visits Tomás's daughter—Duarte's estranged sister—who wants nothing but to be left alone, complicating Isandro's certainty. Reading her mother's final unfinished letter, Isandro finds the sentence her mother never sent: an apology naming Silvestre. The choice crystallizes: silence protected the guilty and starved the innocent alike. Beat: decision under pressure.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe Opens
chapters.summary: Climax. Isandro delivers copies of the archive to a journalist and to Tomás's surviving family, then confronts Silvestre publicly at the family house, reading the final letter aloud. He does not deny it. The town, the family, and Isandro's own carefully invisible life all fracture open. Duarte, given his father's letters at last, weeps without triumph. Beat: truth spoken at cost.

chapters.title: Return Address
chapters.summary: Resolution, months later. The case is reopened quietly; Silvestre faces consequences he accepts. Isandro stays in the town, renting the house—then buying it, her first owned home. She restores the wardrobe as furniture, not shrine. On the anniversary, she writes one final postcard to her mother's burned address, then walks it to the mailbox and lets it go. Beat: belonging chosen, not inherited.
